reason: Signed physician orders for therapy exist for each beneficiary, but the therapy was not shown to be reasonable and necessary. The records show no significant functional gains, and for J.M. a restorative nursing program would have been more appropriate. Daily skilled nursing was also not documented, and an intermittent skilled need does not meet the SNF level of care.

The 12-day hospital stay (Dec 15-27, 2009) meets the 3-day eligibility condition. The record shows fluctuating blood pressure and heart rate requiring at least thirteen medication adjustments and close nursing monitoring, which fits skilled observation and assessment. Two items remain unconfirmed: SNF-side documentation and whether the admission followed discharge directly, so the presumption of coverage cannot be confirmed. The IV fluids and oxygen therapy add support, so coverage rests on the medical evidence.

All three agents found the inpatient admissions unsupported. The RAC found the services belonged in an outpatient setting, and the QIC found the documentation did not support medical necessity for acute hospitalization. The appellant's notice and reopening arguments do not establish coverage, and a contractor's decision on whether to reopen is final and not appealable.

All three agents returned UNKNOWN because the case facts describe only a late extension request and late brief in an appeal. They contain no hospital stay, skilled-care need, or physician certification, so nothing in the record supports SNF coverage.

The billed period (Feb 25–Mar 26, 2006) began after PT (Feb 7, discharged at a plateau) and OT (Feb 24) had ended. The record shows no active skilled therapy plan, maintenance program needing a therapist's skills, or other skilled service for that period. The Eligibility Agent's support rests on the qualifying stay and condition relatedness, which does not establish a skilled level of care during the billed dates.

The beneficiary needs a power wheelchair and staff assistance, and leaving home takes considerable and taxing effort, which matches the policy's stroke/wheelchair example of a homebound patient. His condition did not change, so the nursing notes saying "not homebound" do not defeat homebound status judged over time. The QIC already found the injections reasonable and necessary, and the open questions (details of his absences, facility type, certification) are unresolved rather than adverse.

The SNF claims were denied at every level because the beneficiary was receiving Medicare-covered hospice services on the billed dates (Jan 28 – Mar 1, 2009), and the hospice election was signed Jan 28, 2009. The resident would no longer require skilled care, and nothing in the record shows a daily skilled need unrelated to the terminal condition. The documentation gaps (physician certification, MDS) are unknown and cannot overcome the hospice overlap.

The reviewers denied the visits as non-skilled with no significant change in status. The records instead show medication changes, compliance problems, glucometer difficulty, Humalog compliance management and urinary tract infection monitoring, all handled with skilled nursing assessment and instruction. Skilled care can remain necessary when a patient is stable, so both disputed periods are supported, and the contractor already allowed May 28 to June 20, 2008. Dates before October 1, 2007 were never part of the review and are not decided here.

The physician ordered skilled nursing for one week to monitor for hematuria-related signs. Daily skilled observation and assessment of recurrent bloody urine and abnormal labs, with the physician notified, occurred during March 5-8. A physician had anticipated intermittent hematuria, so there was a reasonable potential for complications, and the SNF admission directly followed the qualifying hospital stay.

The case facts state that the appellant's only argument, based on Jimmo, is unavailing, and the settlement fact sheet is not itself authority. All three agents found no patient facts or documentation showing a need for skilled care, so coverage is not supported.

J.S.'s SNF therapy for September 1-18, 2008 is not supported. The speech therapy notes show only general progress and no treatment method, so they do not show that a skilled professional was needed. The record also lacks PT and OT notes and any documented prior level of function, so a significant functional decline cannot be established. Two agents found the claim unsupported and the third could not confirm eligibility.

All three agents support coverage. The four Lupron skilled nursing visits are backed by a physician's order for injections every 90 days, and nothing in the record contradicts that frequency. The eleven PT visits involved skilled gait training, stair-lift transfer teaching and range-of-motion therapy, all tied to a specific loss of function and documented with measurable improvement.

Skilled nursing wound observation and wound-care teaching is a recognized skilled service. It is supported by the beneficiary's total dependence on his mother as caregiver and by the recurring complications during the dates of service. The documentation agent could not confirm that the required records exist, and the catheter passage was not relied on because the beneficiary has a urostomy and colostomy, not a catheter.

Aide care ordered and furnished at up to 24 hours per day exceeds the part-time or intermittent limit (under 8 hours a day and 28 hours a week, or 35 on case-by-case review). That excess is not covered. Care within the limit could be covered if found reasonable and necessary, but homebound status and plan-of-care documentation are not shown in the facts.

The first stay (9/29/03–11/27/03) is not covered: the physician ordered only intermediate, unskilled nursing facility care with oral medication and a patch, and certified no daily skilled need. The second stay (12/11/03–1/6/04) is supported: signed, dated physician orders require daily IV/IM medication and other skilled services after a qualifying hospital stay. The agents' certification concern is weaker for that stay, and the record shows no valid consent from the daughter or notice for it.

All three agents returned UNKNOWN because the record does not show the preadmission screening, post-admission evaluation, orders or certification, or any clinical facts supporting IRF need. The only affirmative finding is the RAC's determination that the submitted documents did not support the need for IRF services, so coverage is not supported on this record.

All three agents support coverage, and the facts show daily skilled nursing for psychiatric monitoring and for other medical needs (Warfarin discontinuation, pneumonia), plus PT, from August 1 to 11, 2009, after a qualifying hospital stay. After August 11, services were less intensive and the behavioral, cardiac, and pneumonia conditions had stabilized, so the stay is not supported for the rest of August. The PT alone did not support coverage because the mobility problems predated the hospital stay. The agents flagged one unknown, whether an MDS was completed, but nothing in the facts contradicts coverage for August 1-11.

The independent medical expert found the IRF-level criteria were met, and the record supports that. She was admitted two days after a knee replacement with multiple comorbidities, needed IV pain medication and Coumadin adjustments, and was monitored closely by physicians and nursing. She also received daily intensive therapy and made significant functional gains. The agents' open points (rehabilitation physician visit frequency, team conference records, preadmission documents) are not documented in the facts. They are gaps in what the facts show and do not contradict coverage. The QIC's contrary conclusion is outweighed by the specific clinical findings.
